name: Cyproheptadine appetite protocol

card.summary: Use of the antihistamine cyproheptadine, which increases appetite, by people trying to eat more and gain weight or muscle for a fuller physique.
card.note: Prescription-only in the US; causes sedation and anticholinergic effects.

quick.overview:
Cyproheptadine is a first-generation antihistamine and serotonin antagonist that increases appetite and weight as a known effect. People in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles discuss it as a way to eat more when they struggle to reach calorie targets, hoping for a fuller, more muscular physique.

A 2019 systematic review of 46 articles found that most studies reported weight gain with cyproheptadine, though in varied populations such as children, people with cystic fibrosis or cancer, and anorexia nervosa patients.
quick.how: Forum discussions treat it as an appetite aid alongside high-calorie eating and training. It is taken orally; some posters mention it in combination with other compounds. Specific dosing is a matter for a prescriber.
quick.risks: Common effects include sedation, dizziness and dry mouth, and rarer effects include confusion, tremor and liver or blood problems. It is prescription-only in the US and Canada and over the counter in the UK. Appetite-stimulation claims about height are not supported by the cited literature.

lead: Cyproheptadine (brand name Periactin) is a first-generation H1 antihistamine with strong serotonin 5-HT2 antagonist activity, patented in 1959 and introduced medically in 1961 [1]. Increased appetite and weight gain are known effects, and clinicians use it off-label to stimulate appetite in underweight children and people with conditions such as cystic fibrosis [1][2].

In bodybuilding, looksmaxxing and body-shape communities it is discussed as an appetite aid for people who struggle to eat enough to gain weight or muscle, which is the first link in a chain that runs from more food to a gaining phase to a fuller physique [3][4][8]. Parallel uses have spread on social media, where products containing cyproheptadine are promoted for a curvier figure; regulators in the United States and France have issued warnings and restrictions about that use [12][13].

A 2019 systematic review found that 39 of 46 included articles reported significant weight gain, across varied populations such as children, people with cystic fibrosis or cancer, and patients with anorexia nervosa [2]. Trials in healthy people seeking muscle gain have not been published, and discussion of height or hormone effects in forums is separate from this literature.

chain: Weight and, with training, muscle gain
angle.text: People who find it hard to eat enough use appetite stimulation to support a gaining phase, with the physique result depending on diet and training.

Appetite aid for weight or muscle gain

paras: Cyproheptadine blocks histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and has anticholinergic and antidopaminergic properties; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes sedation [1]. It is a tricyclic benzocycloheptene related in structure to pizotifen, ketotifen and tricyclic antidepressants [1]. It is well absorbed by mouth, with peak levels reached after one to four hours and an elimination half-life of about 8.6 hours [1].

Its approved use is for hay fever and other allergic reactions. Documented off-label uses include migraine prevention, serotonin syndrome, antipsychotic-induced akathisia, cyclical vomiting in infants and appetite stimulation [1][5][6]. In 2023 it was the 234th most prescribed drug in the United States, with more than one million prescriptions [1].

Cyproheptadine was patented in 1959 and introduced for medical use in 1961 [1]. Its appetite effect was noticed in allergy and psychiatric patients, and trials in the late 1970s and early 1980s tested it in anorexia nervosa, including a randomized trial of 81 patients reported in 1979 [7]. Editorial commentary in the 1970s and in 2022 has described the drug's wide pharmacological range [1].
Veterinary medicine adopted it too: it is used as an appetite stimulant in cats and as a second-line treatment for pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction in horses [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, members have discussed appetite stimulants for years. A 2007 physique-clinic thread describes cyproheptadine as an antihistamine and serotonin antagonist said to increase appetite and growth hormone secretion, contrasting it with clinical appetite stimulants that posters said mostly add fat [3]. A 2008 thread titled Appetite Stimulants and a 2011 thread on eating more show posters naming Periactin and the antidepressant mirtazapine as aids they had used for low appetite [3][4]. One poster notes that an unusual version of Dianabol sold in the Dominican Republic includes cyproheptadine to raise appetite [3]. A 2026 thread asks about it for chronic low appetite alongside a growth-hormone secretagogue [4].

On looksmax.org, a thread reposting Ray Peat-inspired commentary by the forum figure Haidut lists cyproheptadine with pregnenolone and clonidine as part of an approach to lowering stress; the post links to Peat's view that growth hormone is overrated and sometimes harmful [11]. This community treats the compound in a metabolic and hormonal frame rather than as a simple appetite aid. Claims about height or growth hormone in these discussions are community claims, and the cited literature describes appetite and weight effects.

sections.h: Social media trend and cosmetic weight gain
paras: Outside bodybuilding, cyproheptadine became a social media trend for gaining weight in the chest and hips. In France, TikTok users promoted Periactine as a quick way to gain weight, with before-and-after posts, and one influencer credited it with an hourglass shape after gaining about half a stone in a month [13]. In late June 2024 the French medicines agency announced that from 10 July the drug would be sold only with a prescription, citing misuse for cosmetic weight gain and saying that information measures introduced since 2022 had not stopped it [13].

Apetamin is an unapproved syrup made overseas and sold online, with cyproheptadine as its main active ingredient plus lysine and vitamins B1 and B6 [14]. The US FDA describes it as marketed illegally for weight gain and figure augmentation and says consumers may not know how much cyproheptadine it contains [12]. Poison control sources note that a 2023 customs seizure involved more than 1,000 boxes of apetamin mislabelled as soap [14]. Articles on the trend report experts saying that weight gained on the drug is spread across the body rather than targeted to particular areas [13].

The 2019 Appetite systematic review covered 21 treatment populations and 32 randomized trials; most studies showed weight gain [2]. An early randomized trial in anorexia nervosa found weight gain in a particular subgroup of patients [7]. Pediatric trials in cancer cachexia and feeding disorders have been registered, several terminated early [8][9][10]. The French regulator and a French physician quoted in coverage have described the clinical evidence for weight gain as limited in robustness, which prompted tighter prescribing rules [13].

Reported effects include sedation (often transient), dizziness, confusion, restlessness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention and tachycardia; rare serious effects include liver injury, blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, convulsions and anaphylaxis [1]. The FDA describes sedation, cognitive impairment, dizziness and low blood pressure with Apetamin, and reports of nervous system disorders, irregular heartbeat and liver injury, including one published case of autoimmune hepatitis after six weeks of daily use [12].

Product labels and the FDA note that effects are amplified by alcohol and other central nervous system depressants [1][12]. Contraindications include use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors, angle-closure glaucoma, certain urinary or gastric obstructions, newborns and premature infants, and nursing mothers [1]. Overdose can cause disorientation, hallucinations, convulsions, slowed breathing and coma [12].

Cyproheptadine is prescription-only in the United States and Canada, available over the counter in the UK, pharmacist-only (Schedule 3) in Australia, and since July 2024 prescription-only in France [1][13]. Apetamin is not approved in the US, and the FDA says it is illegally imported [12].

A 2019 systematic review of 46 articles (32 randomized trials) reported significant weight gain in 39 [2]. A 1979 randomized trial in 81 anorexia nervosa patients found weight gain in a subgroup [7]. Registered trials include NCT00066248 in children with cancer-related weight loss, which enrolled 70 participants and was completed, and NCT01132547 and NCT02568007, which were terminated early [8][9][10]. No published trial has tested cyproheptadine for muscle gain in healthy trainees or for height.

lore.intro: Forum members mention cyproheptadine as an appetite aid and, in some threads, a height- or hormone-related tool [3][4][11]. Outside forums, social media promotes it for body shape [13].

claims.claim: It helps people eat more and gain weight
claims.believers: T Nation posters discuss it for low appetite and gaining phases [3][4].
claims.experts: A systematic review found weight gain in most included studies [2].

claims.claim: It raises growth hormone and so helps muscle gain
claims.believers: A 2007 T Nation thread describes it as increasing growth hormone secretion and appetite [3].
claims.experts: The cited literature describes appetite and weight effects; no trial in healthy trainees has measured muscle gain [2].

claims.claim: It affects growth hormone or height
claims.believers: A Ray Peat-inspired thread discusses it alongside other compounds to lower stress and influence hormones [11].
claims.experts: No published studies in the cited literature test cyproheptadine for height.

claims.claim: It adds weight to the chest and hips specifically
claims.believers: French TikTok users post before-and-after photos crediting it with an hourglass figure [13].
claims.experts: Experts quoted in coverage say weight gain on the drug is spread across the body [13].

claims.claim: Apetamin is a harmless vitamin syrup
claims.believers: Sellers market it as a vitamin syrup for a slim-thick figure [14].
claims.experts: The FDA says it is an illegally marketed product containing cyproheptadine in unknown amounts and reports liver injury and nervous system events [12].

claims.claim: It pairs well with other appetite drugs for hard gainers
claims.believers: Posters mention mirtazapine or growth hormone secretagogues alongside it [3][4].
claims.experts: Combining sedating drugs adds sedative effects, and alcohol and other depressants amplify them [1][12].
